subject: Misspecification analysis using MI and EPC

messages.author: bb8109773d780f84
messages.subject: Misspecification analysis using MI and EPC
parts:
Dear all,

I am running a misspecification analysis according to Saris, Satorra & van der Veld (2009) in lavaan using the code

modindices (fit, power = TRUE, delta = .29).

I get modification indices (MI), expected parameter change (EPC) and standardized EPC, on which the decision of misspecification is based. If the MI test is positive and the power of the MI test is high, the size of the EPC is inspected to decide whether the respective path is misspecified or not. I have two questions:

1) Is the EPC or the standardized EPC used for the decision?
2) What is the threshold for the EPC to decide "EPC: m" (misspec.) or "EPC:nm" (not misspec.)?

I get the decision "EPC: nm" for rather large (non.standardized) EPC values and am wondering if I can report it like this or if I need to make some adjustments.

I would appreciate any advise!

Anneke

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Misspecification analysis using MI and EPC
parts: 1) Is the EPC or the standardized EPC used for the decision?

User's choice.  If the original units of the variables involved with the parameter are meaningful, then a reasonable argument could be made for what is "large enough" to consider important.  In the absence of a substantively based threshold, people often rely on SEPC and consider a standardized change of .05 or .10 to be substantial / non-ignorable.
2) What is the threshold for the EPC to decide "EPC: m" (misspec.) or "EPC:nm" (not misspec.)?

|SEPC| > .05 or .10 are arbitrary rules I have seen applied.  What did they use in the article you cited?  See also Whittaker's 2012 study to see what she used.

https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2010.531299

I'm sure there are other sources.  Also see (S)EPC-interest, which can be found using the more general function lavTestScore()

https://www.jstor.org/stable/24573062

Regardless, theoretical motivation for freeing the parameter should be clear, and given more weight in your decision than statistical tools for modification.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
